verses.text: Behold, Yahweh makes the earth empty, makes it waste, turns it upside down, and scatters its inhabitants.

It will be as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the creditor, so with the debtor; as with the taker of interest, so with the giver of interest.
The earth will be utterly emptied and utterly laid waste; for Yahweh has spoken this word.
The earth mourns and fades away. The world languishes and fades away. The lofty people of the earth languish.
The earth also is polluted under its inhabitants, because they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, and broken the everlasting covenant.
Therefore the curse has devoured the earth, and those who dwell therein are found guilty. Therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left.
The new wine mourns. The vine languishes. All the merry-hearted sigh.
The mirth of tambourines ceases. The sound of those who rejoice ends. The joy of the harp ceases.
They will not drink wine with a song. Strong drink will be bitter to those who drink it.
The confused city is broken down. Every house is shut up, that no man may come in.
There is a crying in the streets because of the wine. All joy is darkened. The mirth of the land is gone.
The city is left in desolation, and the gate is struck with destruction.
For it will be so within the earth among the peoples, as the shaking of an olive tree, as the gleanings when the vintage is done.
These shall lift up their voice. They will shout for the majesty of Yahweh. They cry aloud from the sea.
Therefore glorify Yahweh in the east, even the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel, in the islands of the sea!

From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs. Glory to the righteous! But I said, “I pine away! I pine away! woe is me!” The treacherous have dealt treacherously. Yes, the treacherous have dealt very treacherously.
Fear, the pit, and the snare, are on you who inhabitant the earth.

It will happen that he who flees from the noise of the fear will fall into the pit; and he who comes up out of the middle of the pit will be taken in the snare; for the windows on high are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble.
The earth is utterly broken. The earth is torn apart. The earth is shaken violently.
The earth will stagger like a drunken man, and will sway back and forth like a hammock. Its disobedience will be heavy on it, and it will fall and not rise again.
It shall happen in that day that Yahweh will punish the army of the high ones on high, and the kings of the earth on the earth.
They shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison; and after many days shall they be visited.
Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed; for Yahweh of Armies will reign on Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem; and before his elders will be glory.

footnotes.content: The world has always known upheaval—empires crumble, security vanishes, the ground itself seems unstable. Isaiah shows us that behind all of it stands the God who measures out judgment and mercy with one hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When calamity comes, it levels rank and station: priest and people, master and servant, creditor and debtor all share one fate. Isaiah reminds us that before God, we all stand on level ground, equally needy, equally dependent on His mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh has spoken this word"—that clause carries both terror and comfort. Terror, because His word will surely come to pass; comfort, because the God of judgment is also the God who promised never to destroy with silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the mighty languish. The earth itself bows under the weight of sin and its consequence. This isn't poetry for its own sake—it's the testimony that corruption touches everything, and only grace reaches deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The "everlasting covenant"—promised to Noah (Gen 9), binding on all creation—has been broken by those who dwell in it. Isaiah names the crime plainly: we have transgressed, violated, broken. Such honesty about sin is the only gateway to repentance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The curse is not arbitrary—it follows broken covenant as shadow follows substance. Yet even here, not all are consumed. "Few men left" hints that grace preserves a remnant even in judgment; the story doesn't end in emptiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The vine and the new wine mourn—the very symbols of harvest and celebration turn mournful. When joy is stripped away, we learn how much we depended on it, and how desperately we need a joy that can't be taken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tambourines, harps, songs of rejoicing—all fall silent. Isaiah doesn't make judgment pretty. He names the quiet, the hollow absence where music lived, so we understand what's actually at stake when we turn from God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wine once drunk in celebration becomes bitter—not because the vintage is spoiled, but because the heart that would taste it in gratitude has hardened. Judgment strips away the numbing mercies of celebration so we must face ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The "confused city"—places of trade, refuge, and company—becomes a tomb where every door stands shut. Isaiah lifts his eyes to the city as a marker: where there is no welcome, no open hand, mercy has retreated, and desolation enters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A crying in the streets—not from grief now, but from the loss of wine itself, as if hardened hearts weep only for comfort, not for covenant. The prophet shows us what becomes of a people who have forgotten how to grieve rightly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Desolation and destruction mark the city—once a center of life, now a hollow monument to what happens when gates shut and laws are broken. The physical ruin mirrors the spiritual abandonment that preceded it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The olive-tree image speaks of gleaning—what remains after harvest is gathered. Here the theme turns: those few who remain will speak for the Lord, like the smallest olives left behind, but bearing witness still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A sudden turn—those who remain lift up their voice to shout for the majesty of Yahweh. In the darkest hour, a remnant remembers. Their praise comes not from ease or plenty, but from the depth of humbling, and it sounds stronger for it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From east to west, from islands and shores, the call goes out: glorify Yahweh. Even in exile and scattering, the faithful cry out the name of the God of Israel. Their dispersal cannot silence the one truth that holds them together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I pine away! I pine away!" the prophet cries—even amid the singing of the righteous, his heart breaks. This is the prophetic heart: to hold both the praise of the faithful and the sorrow of the fallen in one breath, never choosing numbness over both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear, pit, and snare—three ancient images of entrapment and terror. Isaiah names the tools of destruction plainly, as if to say: judgment is not a vague threat, but a real force that pursues, and only God can deliver us from it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is no escape route—flee one snare and fall into another. Windows burst open above, the earth shakes below; there is no safe place except in the hands of the Judge Himself. Only surrender brings safety.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Broken, torn apart, shaken violently—the earth itself rebels against its inhabitants' sin. Isaiah shows us that creation is not neutral; it protests, it grieves, it cannot long harbor corruption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The earth staggers like a drunk and sways like a hammock—what seemed stable is revealed as fragile. The weight of disobedience pulls it down, and it cannot rise again on its own. Here is the end of self-sufficiency: only grace lifts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The army of the high ones on high, and the kings of the earth"—both the heavenly rebels and earthly tyrants face punishment. Isaiah reveals that what often looks like mighty authority in this world is already marked for judgment in God's court.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prisoners gathered in a pit, locked in darkness for many days—and then "visited." Even this verse, dark as it is, whispers of visitation, as if judgment itself might finally turn to reckoning and restoration. The silence is not final.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of this: Christ reigns on the true Zion, hidden in glory before His elders (His church). Moon and sun grow dim not because creation fails, but because His light outshines them. We live in the age when He reigns and shame touches every false power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
